question: Low visibility operations are defined as take-off and landing operations with an RVR of less than:

options.text: 350 m, the limit below which CAT II operations begin

explanation: Low visibility operations are take-offs and landings with RVR less than 800 m. The CTR VFR limits (5 km, 1500 ft) are a separate matter.

question: Before starting any instrument departure or approach procedure, the pilot must:

options.text: File a new flight plan with the procedure designator and expected time of use
Report visual with the runway
Obtain an ATC clearance
Be at the minimum sector altitude

explanation: Instrument procedures assume conditions below VMC and flight under IFR subject to ATC, so a clearance is required before starting one.

question: A pilot is diverted to an unfamiliar aerodrome and does not have its approach chart. What can ATC do?

options.text: Vector the aircraft to a visual approach only
Nothing; the pilot must not attempt an approach
Provide the procedure by NOTAM before the aircraft reaches the aerodrome, with no lost-communication part
Read out the procedure, including the lost-communication and missed approach procedures

explanation: If a pilot has to divert to an unfamiliar aerodrome without the plates, ATC will read the procedure, including loss of communications and missed approach procedures.

question: In procedure design, obstacle clearance is obtained by:

options.text: Vertical clearance only, as tracking errors are ignored
Lateral containment within a surveyed area and a vertical margin over the obstacles in it
The pilot's own visual lookout during the whole procedure
Lateral clearance only, because the vertical margin is left to the pilot's judgement on the day

explanation: Obstacle clearance combines lateral clearance — the aircraft flown accurately within a surveyed area — and vertical clearance above the obstacles in that area.

question: What happens to the guaranteed obstacle clearance towards the outer edge of a procedure's protected area?

options.text: It increases towards the edge
It stays constant to the edge
It reduces to zero at the outer edge of the secondary area
It doubles at the edge of the area to allow for wind drift and pilot tracking errors

explanation: The full minimum obstacle clearance applies in the primary area and reduces gradually across the secondary area to zero at its outer edge.

question: Obstacle clearance altitude/height (OCA/H) is obtained by:

options.text: Subtracting a margin from the minimum sector altitude
Taking the highest obstacle within 25 NM of the aerodrome reference point
Using the aerodrome elevation plus 1000 ft
Adding a safety margin to the height of the highest relevant obstacle

explanation: OCA/H is the height of the relevant (controlling) obstacle plus a safety margin; this method gives MSA and, with refinements, MDA/H for non-precision procedures.

question: Why is the OCA/H for a precision approach normally lower than for a non-precision approach to the same runway?

options.text: With vertical guidance, an obstacle's significance depends on its range from the threshold
Because precision approaches are flown only by more experienced pilots
Because precision approaches use a higher glide path
Because the obstacle survey for precision approaches only covers the runway strip and its extension

explanation: Precision procedures give height guidance, so a tall obstacle far from the threshold matters less than a low one close in; OCA/H is range dependent and therefore lower.

question: The obstacle clearance used in designing an instrument approach procedure is:

options.text: Generous, so operators can descend below it
The minimum for an acceptable level of safety; operators add margins for their minima
Only advisory for commercial air transport operators
The same as the operator's aerodrome operating minima, so no further margin is ever added by operators

explanation: The published obstacle clearance is considered the minimum required for an acceptable level of safety; operators apply higher criteria to set aerodrome operating minima.

question: Which volume of PANS-OPS (Doc 8168) is intended for flight operations personnel?

options.text: Volume I — Flight Procedures
Volume III — Air Traffic Management
Volume II — Aircraft Operations for crews
Volume II — Construction of Visual and Instrument Flight Procedures

explanation: Volume I (Flight Procedures) is for flight operations personnel; Volume II (Construction of Visual and Instrument Flight Procedures) is for procedure designers.

question: PANS-OPS deals with practices:

options.text: That are binding standards adopted by the Assembly
That apply only to the European region through regional agreements and replace the SARPs there
That replace Annex 6 entirely
Beyond the scope of SARPs, where a measure of international uniformity is desirable

explanation: PANS-OPS covers operational practices beyond the scope of SARPs but where international uniformity is desirable, expanding the SARPs of Annex 6.

question: Instrument departure procedures are designed assuming that:

options.text: The aircraft is at maximum take-off mass with one engine inoperative
One engine has failed at V1
All engines are operating
The aircraft climbs at its maximum rate in still air

explanation: Departure procedures assume all engines operating. Procedures for engine failure after V1 are the operator's responsibility.

question: Besides terrain, which factor may influence the design of a departure procedure?

options.text: The type of fuel used by departing aircraft
ATC requirements, such as adjacent ATS routes or restricted areas
The number of passengers on board
The airline's preferred cruising level and the passenger load factor on the route

explanation: Design is dictated mainly by terrain but may also cater for ATC requirements: adjacent ATS routes, restricted, prohibited or danger areas and nearby aerodromes.

question: When no suitable navigation aid provides track guidance for departure, which criteria are applied?

options.text: Straight departure criteria
Turning departure criteria
Visual departure criteria with the pilot responsible for obstacles
Omnidirectional departure criteria

explanation: Where no suitable navaid gives specific track guidance, omnidirectional (any direction) departure criteria are applied.

question: When is a turning departure constructed?

options.text: Whenever the runway heading differs from the first track by any amount
When the departure route needs a turn of more than 15° to avoid an obstacle
When a turn of more than 30° is required
Only when no navaid is available for a straight departure aligned within 30° of the runway

explanation: A straight departure aligned with the runway is preferred; where a turn of more than 15° is required to avoid an obstacle, a turning departure is constructed.

question: Unless otherwise published, an instrument departure is based on a procedure design gradient (PDG) of:
explanation: Departure procedures are based on an all-engines PDG of 3.3%, or a higher gradient where required for obstacle clearance.

question: A departure route is expressed as tracks to be made good. Under radar vectors, the pilot should:

options.text: Fly the published track and use the vector headings only as a guide
Correct the headings for wind to make good the published track
Fly the headings given, without correcting for wind
Ignore the vectors and fly the published track

explanation: Pilots correct for wind on departure routes defined as tracks, but when radar vectored they fly the vector headings without wind allowance.

question: The 3.3% procedure design gradient is made up of:

options.text: 1.5% for obstacles plus 1.8% for wind and turbulence
2.5% obstacle clearance plus 0.8% for aircraft performance variations with one engine inoperative
3.3% obstacle identification surface with no margin
2.5% obstacle identification surface gradient plus 0.8% increasing obstacle clearance

explanation: The PDG is 2.5% (the OIS gradient, or the gradient based on the critical obstacle if higher) plus 0.8% increasing obstacle clearance.

question: A departure requires a gradient greater than 3.3%. How is this published?

options.text: Only a note that a steep climb is needed
The gradient is given to an altitude/height after which 3.3% is sufficient
The gradient is given as a rate of climb in feet per minute for all speeds
The gradient applies all the way to the cruising level

explanation: Gradients above 3.3% are published to an altitude/height, after which the minimum gradient of 3.3% is considered to exist.

question: Where does an instrument departure procedure end?

options.text: At a significant point where obstacle clearance for the next phase of flight is assured
At the transition altitude in all cases, where the altimeter is set to standard pressure
At the departure end of the runway
At 1500 ft above the aerodrome

explanation: The PDG continues until obstacle clearance is ensured for the next phase (en route, holding or approach); the procedure ends there, marked by a significant point.

question: The minimum obstacle clearance at the departure end of the runway (DER) is:

options.text: 90 m, constant throughout the departure
35 ft, increasing by 2.5% of the distance flown from the DER
Zero, increasing by 0.8% of the horizontal distance flown
300 m, decreasing as the aircraft climbs

explanation: MOC is zero at the DER and increases by 0.8% of the horizontal distance in the direction of flight.

question: In departure design, the area splays out from the departure end of the runway at an angle of:

options.text: 30° on each side
45° on each side
15° on each side
7.5° on each side

explanation: The departure area assumes a maximum divergence of 15° each side of the track.

question: In the turn initiation area of a turning departure, the minimum obstacle clearance provided is:
explanation: A minimum obstacle clearance of 90 m (295 ft) is provided in the turn initiation area; more is added in mountainous terrain.

question: When are increased obstacle clearances applied for mountainous terrain in departure design?

options.text: Whenever the aerodrome is more than 1000 ft above sea level
Only above 10 000 ft elevation
Whenever terrain within 25 NM rises more than 3000 ft above the aerodrome elevation
When an average wind of 37 km/h or more produces significant downdraughts

explanation: Mountainous terrain is not defined; the designer considers prevailing winds, and if an average wind of 37 km/h or more produces significant downdraughts, increased clearance is applied.

question: An aircraft must fly a departure faster than the maximum speed for its category. What should the pilot do?

options.text: Fly the procedure using the next lower category
Request an alternative departure procedure
Reduce bank angle to stay within the protected area
Fly the procedure at the higher speed anyway

explanation: Published limiting speeds must be complied with to stay within the protected areas; if an operation needs a higher speed, an alternative departure must be requested.

question: The maximum speed assumed for a Category C aircraft flying an instrument departure is:

options.text: 165 kt
265 kt
240 kt
290 kt

explanation: Maximum departure speeds are Cat A 120 kt, B 165 kt, C 265 kt, D 290 kt and E 300 kt (IAS).

question: For a straight departure, track guidance must be acquired within what distance of the departure end of the runway?

options.text: 5 km (2.7 NM)

explanation: Straight departures are based on track guidance acquired within 20 km (10.8 NM) of the DER; turning departures within 10 km (5.4 NM) after completing the turn.

question: For a turning departure, track guidance must be acquired within what distance after completing the turn?

options.text: 5 km (2.7 NM)

explanation: For turning departures, track guidance is acquired within 10 km (5.4 NM) after the turn is completed.

question: A straight departure is one in which the initial departure track is within how many degrees of the runway alignment?
explanation: A straight departure has its initial track within 15° of the runway alignment; guidance may be from VOR, NDB or RNAV.

question: In a turning departure, the turn may be specified to start:

options.text: Only at a DME distance
Only overhead a VOR
At an altitude/height, at a fix, or at a facility
Only when the aircraft reaches the minimum sector altitude

explanation: A turning departure turn starts on reaching a specified altitude/height, at a fix, or at a facility (VOR, NDB, etc.).

question: For a turning departure, straight flight is assumed until the aircraft reaches at least what height above the DER elevation?
explanation: Straight flight is assumed until reaching an altitude not less than 120 m (394 ft) above the DER elevation.

question: Who must establish procedures for an engine failure or emergency in flight occurring after V1 during an instrument departure?

options.text: Air traffic control, by publishing them in the AIP
The operator
The State in which the aerodrome lies
The procedure designer

explanation: The operator is responsible for establishing procedures covering engine failure or an emergency in flight after V1.

question: In an omnidirectional departure, the aircraft climbs on the runway centreline before turning to at least:

options.text: 120 m (394 ft) above aerodrome elevation
600 m (1969 ft) above aerodrome elevation
300 m (984 ft) above aerodrome elevation
90 m (295 ft) above aerodrome elevation

explanation: The basic procedure is a climb on the extended centreline to 120 m (394 ft) before turns can be specified.

question: In an omnidirectional departure, before a turn of more than 15° can be made the aircraft must have obstacle clearance of at least:
explanation: At least 90 m (295 ft) of obstacle clearance is provided before turns greater than 15° can be specified.

question: In an omnidirectional departure, turns will not start within what distance of the beginning of the runway?
explanation: Turns will not commence within 600 m of the beginning of the runway.

question: How are restrictions in an omnidirectional departure published?

options.text: As sectors to be avoided, or sectors with minimum gradients and/or altitudes
As a list of obstacles with their heights, for the pilot to plot and avoid before departure
As radar vectors only
As a single straight departure route

explanation: Restrictions are expressed as sectors to be avoided, or sectors with minimum gradients and/or minimum altitudes for safe overflight of obstacles.

question: Obstacles prevent an omnidirectional departure. What alternatives exist?

options.text: Depart with reduced fuel
Depart only at night
Depart only with a radar service provided by the military, following its vectors until clear of terrain
Fly a published departure route, or depart only when ceiling and visibility allow visual obstacle avoidance

explanation: Where obstacles do not permit omnidirectional procedures, a departure route (straight or turning) must be flown, or ceiling and visibility must allow obstacles to be avoided visually.

question: SID charts are published in accordance with the standards of:

options.text: Annex 14 and Annex 15
Annex 10 and Annex 3
Annex 4 and Annex 11
Annex 2 and Annex 6

explanation: Departure routes and SID charts are published according to Annex 11 (ATS) and Annex 4 (Aeronautical Charts).

question: The minimum sector altitude (MSA) shown on charts gives the lowest safe altitude in a sector within what distance of the facility or aerodrome?

options.text: 25 NM
30 NM
10 NM
50 NM

explanation: MSA gives the lowest safe altitude for a defined sector, based on a navigation facility, to a range of 25 NM.

question: Where does a SID start and end?

options.text: At the holding point, ending at the transition altitude
At the runway threshold, ending at the top of climb
At the DER, ending at the first VOR on the route or at the transition altitude, whichever comes first
At the DER, ending where it joins the en-route ATS route system

explanation: All SIDs start at the DER and end at the point where the aircraft joins the ATS en-route system; each has a designator.

question: Which information is shown on a SID chart?

options.text: Aerodrome operating minima
DME distances, radials or QDMs, altitude restrictions, and a narrative in English
Holding speeds for all categories
The approach procedures for each runway end and the aerodrome operating minima for each category

explanation: SIDs specify DME distances, VOR radials or NDB QDMs, altitude restrictions ("above", "at"), a diagram and an English narrative.

question: During a SID, ATC starts radar vectoring the aircraft. What does this mean for the SID?

options.text: It must still be flown in full
The SID altitude restrictions still apply whatever headings are given, until the SID end point is passed
The pilot may choose whether to follow the vectors
It may be abandoned or shortened, and the pilot is told the aircraft is under radar control

explanation: The pilot may be ordered to follow radar vectors, abandoning or abbreviating the SID; the pilot will be told the aircraft is under radar control.

question: To use an RNP-based departure procedure, the aircraft's RNAV system must be:

options.text: Updated with the latest weather data before departure
Coupled to the autopilot throughout
Approved for the published RNP, with the supporting navaids confirmed serviceable
Certified for CAT III approaches, with two independent GNSS receivers coupled to the autopilot

explanation: The RNAV system must be approved for the published RNP, and it must be confirmed before flight that the related navaids (e.g. VOR/DME) are working.

question: Before an RNP departure, the pilot must:

options.text: Request radar vectors for the whole departure
Verify that the aircraft can meet the RNP for the segments to be flown, and monitor accuracy
Obtain written approval from the State of the aerodrome and request radar monitoring of the departure
Disconnect the FMS and fly raw data

explanation: The pilot must verify that the aircraft can meet the RNP requirements for the segments to be flown and continue to monitor system accuracy.

question: Which is one of the four types of turn that may be specified in an RNAV procedure?

options.text: Turn at a fly-over waypoint
Turn at a holding fix only
Turn at a time after take-off
Turn on reaching a specified speed

explanation: RNAV turns may be at a fly-by waypoint, at a fly-over waypoint, at an altitude/height, or a fixed radius turn (mainly for RNP).

question: Can an FMS be used to fly a conventional (non-RNAV) departure procedure?

options.text: No, conventional procedures must always be hand-flown
Yes, without any monitoring
Yes, if monitored on the basic display for that procedure, within raw-data tolerances
Only if ATC approves it for each departure and the procedure is coded as an RNAV departure

explanation: FMS may be used for conventional procedures provided the procedure is monitored on the basic display normally associated with it and raw-data tolerances are complied with.
